title: Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons (1969)
text:
CHAPTER 10. PERCEPTRONS AND THEIR CRITICS
SECTION 10.3. MINSKY AND PAPERT'S PERCEPTRONS (1969)

In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert of MIT published "Perceptrons: An Introduction to Computational Geometry," a mathematical study of what perceptrons can and cannot compute. It is one of the most famous and most misunderstood books in the history of AI. It is often summarized as "they proved perceptrons cannot learn XOR, and that killed neural networks for fifteen years." Both halves of that summary are oversimplified. The XOR limitation of a single linear unit was already well known; the book's real content is a deep theory of the "order" of predicates, proving that certain global properties of images need perceptrons whose units each look at a large part of the image. Whether the book caused the decline of neural network research is still debated. This section explains the actual mathematics, then the history and the controversy.

1. The authors

Marvin Minsky (1927-2016) was a co-founder of the MIT AI Laboratory and one of the organizers of the 1956 Dartmouth workshop (Section 8.2). Ironically, as a student he had built SNARC (1951), one of the first neural network learning machines (Section 7.3), before turning to symbolic AI. Seymour Papert (1928-2016), a mathematician who had worked with Jean Piaget in Geneva, later became famous for the Logo programming language and constructionist education. The book was dedicated to Frank Rosenblatt. The first edition appeared in 1969; a second printing with corrections followed in 1972, and an expanded edition in 1988, after the revival of neural networks, added a prologue and epilogue responding to the new work.

2. Their model of the perceptron

Minsky and Papert studied the perceptron as Rosenblatt's Mark I was built (Section 10.1): a retina R of points (pixels), a set of fixed "partial predicates" phi_1, ..., phi_m (the association units), and a single linear threshold unit:

    psi(X) = 1  if  sum_j a_j phi_j(X) > theta,   else 0

where X is the set of "on" pixels in the image, a_j are learned weights, and each phi_j is an arbitrary Boolean function of the image, but with restrictions on how much of the image it may look at. The question is not whether the learning rule converges (it does, when a solution exists) but whether a solution exists at all, and how large the weights and the number of units must be.

Restrictions studied:

  - Order-limited: each phi_j depends on at most k pixels. The order of a predicate psi is the smallest k for which psi can be represented this way.
  - Diameter-limited: each phi_j depends only on pixels within a small region of the retina.

Low order means "local": each unit sees only a few points. This matches the hope that a perceptron could compute global properties by combining many local pieces of evidence in parallel.

3. Examples of order

  - AND of all pixels ("the image is all black"): a threshold on a sum suffices: psi = 1 iff sum of x_i > |R| - 1/2. Each phi is a single pixel, so order 1. In fact any threshold on the count of pixels is order 1.
  - OR ("at least one pixel on"): order 1, threshold sum > 1/2.
  - XOR of two pixels: order 2. It cannot be done with order 1 (it is not linearly separable), but with the order-2 predicate x1 x2 available: x1 + x2 - 2 x1 x2 > 1/2.
  - Convexity of a figure: Minsky and Papert showed it has low order (order 3 in their analysis), by an argument of this kind: a figure is convex iff for every pair of points in it, the midpoint is also in it, so one can count "bad triples" with order-3 units and threshold on the count being zero.

4. The parity theorem

The parity predicate: psi_par(X) = 1 iff |X|, the number of on pixels, is odd. Theorem (Minsky and Papert): parity has order |R|. That is, a perceptron computing parity must include at least one unit that looks at every pixel of the retina. Local units, no matter how many, cannot do it.

The proof uses a powerful tool, the group invariance theorem. Here is the argument in outline.

Step 1, reduce to masks. Any Boolean function of a set of pixels can be written as a linear combination of masks, the AND of a subset S of pixels: phi_S(X) = 1 iff S is contained in X. (This is like expanding a function as a polynomial in the 0/1 pixel values x_i, where the mask for S is the product of x_i for i in S; since x_i^2 = x_i, every Boolean function is a multilinear polynomial.) So a perceptron of order k can be rewritten as

    psi(X) = 1  iff  sum over |S| <= k of b_S phi_S(X) > theta

Step 2, symmetrize. Parity is invariant under every permutation of the pixels. The group invariance theorem says: if psi is invariant under a group G of permutations and is computable by a perceptron of order k, then it is computable by one of order k in which the coefficients are constant on each orbit of G, that is, all masks that are equivalent under G get the same weight. The proof idea: average the perceptron over all permutations in G. Each permuted perceptron computes the same psi (by invariance), and an average of sums that are all above theta (or all at most theta) stays on the same side, so the averaged perceptron still computes psi, and its coefficients are now symmetric. (Strict inequalities and finiteness of G make this work.)

Step 3, use the symmetry. Under the full permutation group, all masks of the same size are equivalent. So the weight of a mask depends only on its size j. Then

    sum_S b_S phi_S(X) = sum_{j=0..k} c_j * (number of j-subsets of X) = sum_j c_j C(|X|, j)

where C(n, j) is the binomial coefficient. This is a polynomial P(n) of degree at most k in n = |X|.

Step 4, count sign changes. The perceptron says "odd" iff P(n) > theta. As n goes 0, 1, 2, ..., |R|, parity alternates, so P(n) - theta must change sign |R| times. A polynomial of degree k changes sign at most k times (it has at most k real roots). Hence k >= |R|. QED.

So parity requires a unit of maximal order. Moreover, Minsky and Papert showed the coefficients needed for some such problems grow very fast with the retina size, making the representation impractical even if it exists.

5. Connectedness

The other famous result concerns connectedness: is the figure in the image one connected piece? Minsky and Papert proved that connectedness is not of bounded order: for any fixed k, there are large enough retinas on which no order-k perceptron computes it. Their argument reduces a parity-like problem to connectedness, using an image built from a grid of strips whose switching pattern connects or disconnects the figure depending on the parity of certain pixels, so a low-order perceptron for connectedness would give a low-order one for parity. They also showed that connectedness is not computable by diameter-limited perceptrons. The book's cover shows two spiral-like figures, one connected and one not, which are hard for humans to tell apart at a glance: a hint that this kind of global property is difficult in general, and that serial tracing is a natural method for it.

The deeper point: properties that depend on the whole figure in a global way are fundamentally hard for a single layer of local feature detectors followed by a linear vote. By contrast, a property like "the number of on pixels is at least 10" is easy.

6. What the book said about multilayer networks

The book focused on single-layer perceptrons (one adaptive layer over fixed features). It did not prove that multilayer networks were useless. But it expressed doubt about them. In a widely quoted passage near the end, the authors conjectured that extending the perceptron to multilayer systems would be "sterile," while acknowledging that this was an intuitive judgment and an important open problem. They also discussed "Gamba machines" (a perceptron with an extra layer of perceptrons in front) and conjectured these would need an enormous number of units.

Rosenblatt himself had already studied multilayer perceptrons in "Principles of Neurodynamics" (1962), and had shown that an elementary perceptron with an unlimited number of association units could represent any classification. The problem was not representation but learning: nobody had a reliable method to train the hidden layers. Minsky and Papert's pessimism concerned exactly that.

7. Reception and influence

The book's influence is the subject of real historical debate.

The traditional story: the book's prestige and rigorous negative results persuaded funding agencies and researchers that neural networks were a dead end, and research largely stopped until the 1980s. Funding did move strongly toward symbolic AI in the 1970s, and neural network research did decline.

Complications:

  - Other factors contributed. Rosenblatt died in 1971. Early hardware was limited, and the hype around perceptrons had produced disappointment. AI funding in general was cut in the early 1970s (the Mansfield Amendment in the US, the Lighthill report in the UK; Chapter 11), affecting symbolic AI too.
  - Neural network research did not stop. Throughout the 1970s, researchers including Stephen Grossberg, Teuvo Kohonen, Shun-ichi Amari, Kunihiko Fukushima (whose Neocognitron of 1980 is an ancestor of convolutional networks) and others continued, though with less visibility and funding. Paul Werbos described backpropagation for neural networks in his 1974 PhD thesis.
  - Reviewers at the time pointed out the book's limited scope. Reviews appeared promptly (for example by Michael Arbib in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 1969), and some commentators argued the book studied a severely limited class of machines from a viewpoint different from Rosenblatt's, so its title was misleading.

When neural networks returned in the mid-1980s, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed that backpropagation could train multilayer networks to solve XOR and parity (Chapter 13), and the PDP group wrote that Minsky and Papert's pessimism about learning in multilayer machines had been misplaced. In the 1988 expanded edition, Minsky and Papert replied that the new results did not overturn their analysis: multilayer networks trained by gradient descent were still limited, scaling was unproven, and the essential problems (like parity and connectedness) remained hard. They argued that much of the new work repeated claims without the mathematical analysis that would show whether it scaled.

8. The view from 2026

Both sides were partly right.

  - Minsky and Papert's theorems are correct and still matter. Parity is genuinely hard for many learning methods: learning parity of k bits out of n with gradient descent needs resources growing roughly like n^k in common theoretical models, and "learning parities" is a standard example of a problem that is hard for gradient-based learning in the absence of special structure. Transformers trained on arithmetic and parity tasks also show difficulties with length generalization.
  - Their central insight, that a computing architecture's structure determines what it can efficiently compute, is the foundation of modern work on the expressive power of networks: depth separation results (functions that deep networks compute with few units but shallow networks need exponentially many), and circuit-complexity analyses of what transformers can compute in a fixed number of layers.
  - But their pessimism about multilayer learning was wrong in practice. With differentiable units, backpropagation, large datasets and GPU computation (Chapters 13-16), multilayer networks became the dominant approach to AI. Connectedness-like and global properties are handled by depth: a deep network can compute global properties through many layers of local operations, just as a convolutional network's receptive field grows with depth, and recurrence or iteration can implement serial procedures like tracing.

The parity proof also shows why depth helps: parity of n bits is easy with a chain or tree of XOR gates of depth about log2(n), each looking at only two inputs. The limitation is specific to one layer of local features plus one linear threshold.

9. Summary

  - "Perceptrons" (Minsky and Papert, MIT, 1969; expanded edition 1988) analyzed single-layer perceptrons over fixed partial predicates.
  - The order of a predicate is the size of the largest unit needed. Counting thresholds are order 1, XOR is order 2, convexity is low order.
  - Using the group invariance theorem and a polynomial sign-change argument, they proved parity has order equal to the retina size; connectedness is not of bounded order.
  - They conjectured that multilayer extensions would be "sterile," a judgment about learning that proved wrong in practice once backpropagation was adopted.
  - The book contributed to the 1970s decline of neural network funding, though historians debate how much; research continued at a lower level.
  - Its mathematics remains relevant to modern questions about the expressive power and learnability of networks.
